verses.37:1: Now Bezalel also made the ark of acacia wood, having two and a half cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width; the height also was one cubit and a half, and he overlaid it with the purest gold inside and out.
verses.37:2: And he made for it a golden crown all around,
verses.37:3: casting four golden rings at its four corners: two rings on one side, and two on the other.
verses.37:4: He also made the poles of acacia wood, which he overlaid with gold,
verses.37:5: and which he put into the rings that were on the sides of the ark to carry it.
verses.37:6: He also made the mercy seat, that is, the oracle, of the purest gold, two and a half cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width;
verses.37:7: also two cherubim of hammered gold, which he placed on each side of the mercy seat:
verses.37:8: one cherub at the end of one side, and the other cherub at the end of the other side—two cherubim on the respective ends of the mercy seat,
verses.37:9: stretching out their wings and covering the mercy seat, looking toward one another and toward it.
verses.37:10: He also made the table of acacia wood, two cubits in length and one cubit in width, which had a cubit and a half in height.
verses.37:11: And he overlaid it with the purest gold, and made for it a golden rim all around,
verses.37:12: and for the rim itself a carved golden crown of four fingers, and upon the same, another golden crown.
verses.37:13: He also cast four golden rings, which he placed at the four corners by each of the feet of the table
verses.37:14: opposite the crown; and he put poles into them so that the table could be carried.
verses.37:15: The poles themselves he also made of acacia wood, and overlaid them with gold;
verses.37:16: and the vessels for the various uses of the table: dishes, bowls, cups, and censers, of pure gold, in which the drink offerings are to be offered.
verses.37:17: He also made the hammered lampstand of the purest gold, from whose shaft branches, cups, small spheres, and lilies extended:
verses.37:18: six on both sides, three branches on one side, and three on the other:
verses.37:19: Three cups in the shape of a nut were on each branch, and small spheres together with lilies; and three cups like a nut on the other branch, and small spheres together with lilies. The workmanship of the six branches that extended from the stem of the lampstand was uniform.
verses.37:20: Now on the shaft itself there were four cups in the shape of a nut, and small spheres on each one together with lilies,
verses.37:21: and small spheres under two branches in three places, which together make six branches proceeding from one shaft.
verses.37:22: Therefore both the small spheres and the branches were from it, all of them hammered work of the purest gold.
verses.37:23: He also made seven lamps with their snuffers, and the vessels where what has been snuffed may be extinguished, of the purest gold.
verses.37:24: The lampstand, along with all its vessels, weighed a talent of gold.
verses.37:25: He also made the altar of incense of acacia wood, measuring one cubit square and two in height, from whose corners horns extended.
verses.37:26: And he covered it with the purest gold, along with the grate, the walls, and the horns.
verses.37:27: And he made for it a small gold crown all around, and two gold rings beneath the crown on each side, so that poles could be inserted into them and the altar could be carried.
verses.37:28: The poles themselves, however, he made of acacia wood and overlaid with gold plates.
verses.37:29: He also compounded the oil for the ointment of sanctification, and the incense of the purest spices by the work of a perfumer.
verses.38:1: He also made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood, five cubits square, and three in height:
verses.38:2: whose horns extended from the corners, and he overlaid it with bronze plates.
verses.38:3: And for its uses he prepared various vessels of bronze: pots, tongs, forks, hooks, and receptacles for fire.
verses.38:4: And he made its bronze grating in the manner of a net, and beneath it in the middle of the altar a hearth,
verses.38:5: having cast four rings at the same number of ends of the network, for inserting the poles to carry it,
verses.38:6: which he also made of acacia wood and overlaid with bronze plates:
verses.38:7: and he inserted them into the rings that projected from the sides of the altar. The altar itself, however, was not solid, but hollow, made of boards, and empty inside.
verses.38:8: He also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the doorway of the tabernacle.
verses.38:9: He also made the courtyard, on whose southern side there were hangings of twisted fine linen, of one hundred cubits,
verses.38:10: twenty bronze pillars with their bases; the capitals of the pillars and all the engraved work were of silver.
verses.38:11: Likewise on the northern side the hangings, pillars, bases, and capitals of the pillars were of the same measurement, workmanship, and metal.
verses.38:12: Now on the side that faces the west, there were hangings of fifty cubits, ten bronze pillars with their bases, and the capitals of the pillars and all the engraved work were of silver.
verses.38:13: Furthermore, toward the east he prepared hangings of fifty cubits:
verses.38:14: of which one side held fifteen cubits belonging to three pillars, with their bases;
verses.38:15: and on the other side (because between the two he made the entrance of the tabernacle) there were likewise hangings of fifteen cubits, and three pillars, and the same number of bases.
verses.38:16: All the hangings of the courtyard had been woven of twisted fine linen.
verses.38:17: The bases of the pillars were of bronze, but their capitals, with all their engravings, were of silver; and he even covered the pillars of the courtyard themselves with silver.
verses.38:18: And at its entrance he made a hanging with embroidered work of blue, purple, crimson, and twisted fine linen, which had twenty cubits in length, while the height was five cubits, according to the measurement that all the hangings of the courtyard had.
verses.38:19: Now the pillars at the entryway were four, with bronze bases, and their capitals and engravings were of silver.
verses.38:20: He also made the pegs of the tabernacle and of the courtyard all around of bronze.
verses.38:21: These are the furnishings of the tabernacle of the testimony, which were counted according to the command of Moses in the ceremonies of the Levites by the hand of Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest,
verses.38:22: which Bezalel, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, had completed as the Lord commanded through Moses,
verses.38:23: with Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, joined to him as a partner, who was himself also an outstanding craftsman in wood, and a weaver of patterned work and an embroiderer in blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen.
verses.38:24: All the gold that was spent in the work of the sanctuary, and that was offered in gifts, was twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels, according to the measure of the sanctuary.
verses.38:25: Now it was offered by those who passed to the numbering, from twenty years old and upward, from six hundred three thousand, five hundred and fifty armed men.
verses.38:26: Moreover, there were one hundred talents of silver from which were cast the bases of the sanctuary, and of the entrance where the veil hangs.
verses.38:27: One hundred bases were made from one hundred talents, with one talent reckoned for each base.
verses.38:28: Now from the one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five, he made the capitals of the pillars, and the pillars themselves he also overlaid with silver.
verses.38:29: Of bronze also there were offered seventy-two thousand talents, and four hundred shekels in addition,
verses.38:30: from which were cast the bases at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony, and the bronze altar with its grating, and all the vessels that belong to its use,
verses.38:31: and the bases of the courtyard both around it and at its entrance, and the pegs of the tabernacle and of the courtyard all around.
verses.39:1: Now of blue and purple, crimson and fine linen, he made the garments in which Aaron was to be clothed when he ministered in the holy places, just as the Lord commanded Moses.
verses.39:2: Therefore he made the shoulder vestment of gold, blue, and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen,
verses.39:3: with patterned weaving; and he cut thin gold sheets and drew them out into threads, so that they could be twisted with the weft of the preceding colors,
verses.39:4: and two borders joined to one another on both sides of the upper edges,
verses.39:5: and a belt of the same colors, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.39:6: He also prepared two onyx stones, fastened and enclosed in gold, and engraved by the craft of a gem-engraver with the names of the sons of Israel;
verses.39:7: and he placed them on the sides of the shoulder vestment as a memorial of the sons of Israel, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.39:8: He also made the breastpiece with patterned weaving, like the work of the shoulder vestment, of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen,
verses.39:9: four-cornered, doubled, of a palm's measure.
verses.39:10: And he set in it four rows of gems. In the first row were a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald.
verses.39:11: In the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper.
verses.39:12: In the third, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst.
verses.39:13: In the fourth, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl, surrounded and enclosed in gold in their rows.
verses.39:14: And those twelve stones were engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, each one according to each individual name.
verses.39:15: They also made on the breastpiece small chains linked to one another, of purest gold,
verses.39:16: and two hooks, and the same number of gold rings. Moreover, they placed the rings on both sides of the breastpiece,
verses.39:17: from which two gold chains were to hang, which they inserted into the hooks that projected at the corners of the shoulder vestment.
verses.39:18: These fit together with one another both in front and behind in such a way that the shoulder vestment and the breastpiece were bound to each other,
verses.39:19: drawn tight to the belt and more firmly joined by the rings, which a blue cord connected, so that they would not hang loosely and shift away from one another, just as the Lord commanded Moses.
verses.39:20: And they also made the tunic of the shoulder vestment entirely violet-blue,
verses.39:21: and an opening for the head in the upper part at the middle, and a woven border all around the opening;
verses.39:22: and below, at the feet, pomegranates of blue, purple, crimson, and twisted fine linen;
verses.39:23: and bells of purest gold, which they placed between the pomegranates at the bottom edge of the tunic all around:
verses.39:24: a gold bell and a pomegranate, with which the high priest walked adorned when he performed his ministry, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.39:25: They also made tunics of fine linen with woven work for Aaron and his sons;
verses.39:26: and turbans with their little crowns, of fine linen;
verses.39:27: also linen undergarments, of fine linen;
verses.39:28: and a sash of twisted fine linen, blue, purple, and twice-dyed crimson, with the craft of embroidery, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.39:29: They also made the plate of sacred veneration of purest gold, and they wrote on it with the work of a gem-engraver, "Holiness of the Lord,"
verses.39:30: and they bound it to the turban with a blue cord, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.39:31: Therefore all the work of the tabernacle and of the tent of the testimony was completed, and the sons of Israel did all that the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.39:32: And they presented the tabernacle and the tent and all the furnishings: the rings, the boards, the bars, the pillars, and the bases,
verses.39:33: the covering of rams' skins dyed red, and another covering of violet-colored skins,
verses.39:34: the veil; the ark, the poles, the mercy seat,
verses.39:35: the table with its vessels and the loaves of presentation;
verses.39:36: the lampstand, the lamps, and their utensils with the oil;
verses.39:37: the golden altar, and the ointment, and the incense of spices,
verses.39:38: and the hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle;
verses.39:39: the bronze altar, the grating, the poles, and all its vessels; the basin with its base; the hangings of the courtyard, and the pillars with their bases;
verses.39:40: the hanging at the entrance of the courtyard, and its cords and pegs. Nothing was lacking of the vessels that were ordered to be made for the service of the tabernacle and for the tent of the covenant.
verses.39:41: The garments also that the priests use in the sanctuary, namely, Aaron and his sons,
verses.39:42: the sons of Israel presented, just as the Lord had commanded.
verses.39:43: After Moses saw that all these things were completed, he blessed them.
verses.40:1: And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
verses.40:2: "In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall erect the tabernacle of the testimony,
verses.40:3: and you shall place the ark in it, and let down the veil before it;
verses.40:4: and when the table has been brought in, you shall place upon it the things that have been duly commanded. The lampstand shall stand with its lamps,
verses.40:5: and the golden altar, on which incense is burned, before the ark of the testimony. You shall place the hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle,
verses.40:6: and before it the altar of burnt offering:
verses.40:7: the basin between the altar and the tabernacle, which you will fill with water.
verses.40:8: And you shall surround the courtyard with hangings, and its entrance.
verses.40:9: And having taken the oil of anointing, you shall anoint the tabernacle with its vessels, so that they may be sanctified:
verses.40:10: the altar of burnt offering and all its vessels,
verses.40:11: the basin with its base; you will consecrate all of them with the anointing oil, so that they will be most holy.
verses.40:12: And you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the doors of the tabernacle of the testimony, and when they have been washed with water,
verses.40:13: you shall clothe them with holy garments, so that they may minister to Me, and their anointing may serve for an everlasting priesthood."
verses.40:14: And Moses did all that the Lord had commanded.
verses.40:15: Therefore, in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was set in place.
verses.40:16: And Moses erected it, and placed the boards and bases and bars, and set up the pillars,
verses.40:17: and spread the tent over the tabernacle, with the covering placed on top, just as the Lord had ordered.
verses.40:18: He also placed the testimony in the ark, with the poles placed underneath, and the oracle on top.
verses.40:19: And when he had brought the ark into the tabernacle, he hung the veil before it so that he might fulfill the order of the Lord.
verses.40:20: He also placed the table in the tabernacle of the testimony on the north side outside the veil,
verses.40:21: with the loaves of presentation arranged in order in front, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.40:22: He also placed the lampstand in the tabernacle of the testimony opposite the table on the south side,
verses.40:23: with the lamps set in order, according to the command of the Lord.
verses.40:24: He also placed the golden altar under the tent of the testimony facing the veil,
verses.40:25: and burned incense of spices upon it, just as the Lord had ordered Moses.
verses.40:26: He also placed the hanging at the entryway of the tabernacle of the testimony,
verses.40:27: and the altar of burnt offering in the entryway of the testimony, offering on it the burnt offering and the sacrifices, as the Lord had ordered.
verses.40:28: He also set up the basin between the tabernacle of the testimony and the altar, filling it with water.
verses.40:29: And Moses and Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet,
verses.40:30: when they entered the tent of the covenant and approached the altar, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.
verses.40:31: He also erected the courtyard all around the tabernacle and the altar, with the hanging drawn across its entrance. After all things were completed,
verses.40:32: a cloud covered the tabernacle of the testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it.
verses.40:33: Nor was Moses able to enter the tent of the covenant, with the cloud covering everything and the majesty of the Lord flashing forth, because the cloud had covered all things.
verses.40:34: Whenever the cloud left the tabernacle, the sons of Israel set out by their companies:
verses.40:35: if it hung above, they stayed in the same place.
verses.40:36: For the cloud of the Lord rested upon the tabernacle by day, and fire in the night, with all the peoples of Israel watching throughout all their encampments.

notes.1:7: Latin "quasi germinantes" ("as though sprouting forth") renders the Hebrew verb for swarming or teeming with a botanical image of rapid growth.
notes.1:11: Latin "urbes tabernaculorum" ("cities of tabernacles") is a distinctly Vulgate rendering, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "store cities" and the Septuagint reads "fortified cities."
notes.1:16: Latin "et partus tempus advenerit" ("and the time of birth has come") renders by sense the difficult Hebrew phrase "upon the two stones" (apparently a birthstool).
notes.1:19: Latin "ipsae enim obstetricandi habent scientiam" ("for they themselves have the knowledge of midwifery") is a distinctive Vulgate reading, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text says that they are "lively" (vigorous).
notes.2:14: Latin "Quomodo palam factum est verbum istud?" presents Moses's reaction as a question ("How has this matter become publicly known?"), aligning with the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew Masoretic statement ("Surely the matter is known").
notes.2:19: Latin "nobiscum" ("with us") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "for us."
notes.2:21: Latin "Juravit" ("swore") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text means "agreed" or "was content," and "Accepitque" ("and he took") makes Moses the subject rather than Reuel giving Zipporah to him.
notes.2:22: The Clementine Vulgate (with some Septuagint and Old Latin witnesses) includes the birth and naming of Eliezer here, which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text in this verse and appears later in Exodus 18:4.
notes.3:2: Latin "Dominus" ("the Lord") appears directly without "angel of," whereas both the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Septuagint read "the angel of the Lord."
notes.3:12: Latin "immolabis" ("you will sacrifice") uses a second-person singular verb specifically denoting sacrifice, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the second-person plural "you shall serve."
notes.3:14: Latin "Qui est" ("He Who Is") is a third-person formulation shared with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text repeats the first-person form ("I am").
notes.3:18: Latin "vocavit nos" ("has called us") agrees with the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "has met with us."
notes.3:22: Latin "hospita" can denote either a female houseguest/lodger staying in the home (matching the Hebrew expression for a woman sojourning in the house) or a hostess.
notes.4:12: Latin in ore tuo ("in your mouth"; likewise in 4:15) is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew reads "with your mouth."
notes.4:13: Latin mitte quem missurus es ("send the one whom You are going to send") uses the future active participle; the Hebrew reads "send by the hand of whom You will send."
notes.4:16: Latin in his quae ad Deum pertinent ("in those things that pertain to God") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Hebrew literally reads "as God."
notes.4:25: Latin acutissimam petram ("a very sharp stone") renders the Hebrew "flint," and Sponsus sanguinum ("a bridegroom of blood," literally plural "of bloods") preserves a famously difficult idiom whose precise referent remains debated.
notes.5:3: Latin vocavit nos ("has called us") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Hebrew reads "has met with us."
notes.5:5: Latin videtis quod turba succreverit: quanto magis si dederitis eis requiem ab operibus? ("you see that the crowd has increased; how much more if you give them rest from work?") is a distinctly Vulgate expansion and question compared with the shorter Hebrew clause.
notes.5:12: Latin ad colligendas paleas ("to gather straw") simplifies the Hebrew phrase "to gather stubble for straw."
notes.5:16: Latin et injuste agitur contra populum tuum ("and injustice is done against your people") is a Vulgate-distinct reading where the Hebrew literally says "and the fault is your own people's."
notes.6:3: Latin literally reads "in God Almighty" (in Deo omnipotente), reflecting the Hebrew idiom for appearing in that character. For the divine name, the Vulgate uses Adonai here rather than a form of the Tetragrammaton.
notes.6:6: Latin ergastulo (also in v. 7) refers to a slave prison or forced-labor workhouse, a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew has "burdens." Likewise, "an uplifted arm" translates Vulgate brachio excelso (literally "high" or "lofty arm") rather than the Hebrew "outstretched arm."
notes.6:12: The literal idiom "uncircumcised in lips" (also in v. 30) signifies faltering or unready speech; the Vulgate also adds praesertim ("especially") here.
notes.6:20: The Vulgate identifies Jochebed as patruelem suam ("his paternal cousin," agreeing with the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text identifies her as his father's sister (his aunt).
notes.7:1: Latin Deum Pharaonis (literally "God of Pharaoh," where the Hebrew has "God to Pharaoh") signifies that Moses will stand in God's place with authority over Pharaoh while Aaron speaks as his prophet.
notes.7:10: The Vulgate reads tulit ("took"), whereas the Hebrew says Aaron cast down his staff.
notes.7:12: The Vulgate shifts from colubrum ("serpent," vv. 9-10) to dracones/draconem ("dragons"/"dragon," vv. 12, 15), where the Hebrew uses a single term throughout.
notes.7:13: The Vulgate reads sicut praeceperat Dominus ("just as the Lord had commanded," also in v. 22), whereas the Hebrew has "as the Lord had spoken."
notes.8:1: Native Vulgate Exodus 8:1-4 (the warning of the plague of frogs) map to Saints.Bible 7:26-29, and native Vulgate 8:5-32 map to Saints.Bible 8:1-28.
notes.8:3: The Vulgate translates "into the remains of your food" (in reliquias ciborum tuorum) where the Hebrew has "into your kneading bowls." Native Vulgate Exodus 8:1-4 map to Saints.Bible 7:26-29.
notes.8:5: As in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, chapter 8 of this Latin text begins at the command to stretch out Aaron's hand, because the preceding warning about frogs appears at 7:26-29; thus chapter 8 has 28 verses rather than the 32 of the alternative numbering, in which this verse is 8:5.
notes.8:12: The Vulgate reads pro sponsione ranarum quam condixerat Pharaoni ("regarding the promise about the frogs that he had agreed upon with Pharaoh," reflecting the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew text reads "because of the frogs that He had brought upon Pharaoh."
notes.8:15: The Vulgate renders "just as the Lord had commanded" (praeceperat, also in 8:15 and 9:35), whereas the Hebrew reads "just as the Lord had spoken." It also distinguishes ingravare ("make heavy," 8:11, 8:28, 9:7, 9:35) from indurare ("harden," 8:15, 9:12, 9:35).
notes.8:21: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for a swarm or mixture of insects as "every kind of fly" (omne genus muscarum) and "flies of various kinds" (muscis diversi generis), and uses collective singular musca in 8:20 and 8:25.
notes.8:26: The Vulgate clarifies the second clause with ea quae colunt Aegyptii ("the things that the Egyptians worship") and casts the conclusion as a statement ("they will overwhelm us with stones") rather than the Hebrew rhetorical question ("will they not stone us?").
notes.9:3: The Vulgate reads super agros tuos ("upon your fields"), whereas the Hebrew text specifies "upon your livestock that are in the field."
notes.9:4: As in 8:18 (Faciamque mirabilem ... terram Gessen, "I will make marvelous the land of Goshen"), the Vulgate reads faciet Dominus mirabile ("the Lord will do a marvelous thing") and possessiones ("possessions"), where the Hebrew emphasizes "setting apart" Israel's "livestock."
notes.9:15: As in the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses future indicatives (percutiam ... peribisque, "I will strike ... and you will perish"), whereas the Hebrew uses past forms, generally understood as counterfactual ("I could have struck ... and you would have been cut off").
notes.9:31: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew crop terms ("in the ear" and "in bud") as virens ("green") and folliculos germinaret ("putting forth pods").
notes.9:35: The Vulgate combines both hardening verbs in the passive voice in a single clause (ingravatum est ... et induratum nimis, "was made heavy and exceedingly hardened") and places the mention of Pharaoh's servants here rather than in 9:34.
notes.10:2: Latin "quoties contriverim Ægyptios" ("how many times I have crushed the Egyptians") is a distinct Vulgate rendering; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "how I have dealt harshly with / made sport of the Egyptians," and also has a singular "son's son" where the Vulgate has plural "nepotum" ("grandsons").
notes.10:7: Latin "patiemur hoc scandalum" ("will we endure this stumbling block") differs in subject and phrasing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which asks "how long will this [man] be a snare to us?"
notes.10:10: Latin "cui dubium est quod pessime cogitetis?" ("Who doubts that you are plotting most wickedly?") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering of the Hebrew idiom "see, evil is before your face."
notes.10:13: Latin "ventum urentem" ("a scorching wind") characterizes the Hebrew "east wind" (the hot desert sirocco) by its burning effect rather than its compass direction.
notes.10:15: Latin "vastantes omnia" ("devastating everything") diverges from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "and the land was darkened."
notes.11:3: Latin uses the future tense "Dabit" ("will give"), continuing the Lord's promise from verse 2, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses the narrative past ("gave").
notes.11:7: Latin "non mutiet canis" ("not a dog will make a sound") uses a classical idiom for uttering even the faintest sound or growl, rendering the Hebrew expression "will not sharpen its tongue."
notes.11:8: Latin has first-person plural "egrediemur" ("we will go out") where the Hebrew has singular "I will go out," and renders "who follow at your feet" as "qui subjectus est tibi" ("who are subject to you"). In the Vulgate verse division, Moses' angry departure opens verse 9 rather than closing verse 8.
notes.11:10: Latin "quæ scripta sunt" ("that are written") is a distinct Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text simply has "all these wonders."
notes.12:8: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "bitter herbs" (merorim) specifically as lactucis agrestibus ("wild lettuce").
notes.12:11: The Vulgate transliterates Hebrew Pesach as Phase and inserts the explanatory gloss (id est, transitus), "that is, the passing over," which does not appear in the Hebrew text.
notes.12:22: The Vulgate reads in limine ("on the threshold"), reflecting one meaning of the ambiguous Hebrew noun saph, which can also mean "basin."
notes.12:29: The Vulgate specifies the feminine captivae ("the captive woman who was in prison"), whereas the Hebrew uses the masculine singular ("the captive who was in the dungeon").
notes.12:48: The Vulgate uses Roman civic terms, in vestram coloniam ("into your settlement") here and colono ("settler") in v. 49, where the Hebrew speaks simply of a stranger sojourning with Israel.
notes.13:4: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew month name Abib descriptively as mense novarum frugum ("the month of new crops").
notes.13:10: Latin a diebus in dies ("from days to days") preserves the literal Hebrew idiom for an annual recurrence ("year by year").
notes.13:13: The Vulgate generalizes the Hebrew "break its neck" to interficies ("you will kill it") and adds pretio ("with a price") for the redemption of a human firstborn.
notes.13:16: For the Hebrew totaphot ("frontlets"), the Vulgate reads quasi appensum quid, ob recordationem ("like something hung, for remembrance").
notes.13:21: Where the Hebrew speaks of giving light so Israel could travel by day and night, the Vulgate reads ut dux esset itineris utroque tempore ("so that He might be the guide of the journey at both times").
notes.14:3: Latin coarctati sunt ("they are hemmed in") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Hebrew means "they are wandering in confusion."
notes.14:9: The Vulgate adds vestigia praecedentium ("the tracks of those going ahead") and renders Hebrew "overtook" as repererunt ("they found").
notes.14:13: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "salvation of the Lord" as magnalia Domini ("the great works of the Lord").
notes.14:21: Latin vento vehementi et urente ("a strong and burning wind") interprets the Hebrew "strong east wind" as a scorching wind, and abstulit ("removed") stands in place of "drove back."
notes.14:24: The Vulgate reads interfecit exercitum eorum ("killed their army") and in 14:25 subvertit rotas ... ferebanturque in profundum ("overturned the wheels ... and they were carried into the deep"), differing from the Hebrew "threw the army into panic" and "removed/bound their wheels so that they drove heavily."
notes.15:3: The Vulgate reads 'quasi vir pugnator, Omnipotens nomen ejus' ("like a fighting man; Almighty is His name"), adding the comparative "like" and rendering the second occurrence of the divine name as "Almighty" rather than repeating "the Lord."
notes.15:11: Latin 'in fortibus' ("among the mighty") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew reads "among the gods."
notes.15:14: The Vulgate reads 'Ascenderunt populi, et irati sunt' ("The peoples went up and became angry"), differing markedly from the Hebrew ("The peoples heard; they tremble").
notes.15:19: Latin 'eques Pharao' depicts Pharaoh entering the sea "on horseback" as a rider, whereas the Hebrew refers to "the horses of Pharaoh."
notes.15:23: The Vulgate explicitly explains the etymology of Marah with 'congruum loco nomen imposuit ... id est, amaritudinem' ("assigned a fitting name to the place ... that is, bitterness").
notes.16:14: The Vulgate reads 'Cumque operuisset superficiem terrae' ("when it had covered the surface of the earth," rather than when the dew lifted) and renders the rare Hebrew descriptor with 'quasi pilo tusum' ("as if pounded with a pestle").
notes.16:15: Latin 'Manhu' transliterates the Hebrew exclamation 'man hu' ("What is it?"), which the Vulgate immediately glosses as 'Quid est hoc?' ("What is this?").
notes.16:16: The Latin dry measure 'gomor' (like 'ephi' in 16:36) is rendered using the standard modern English spelling "omer" (and "ephah").
notes.16:31: The Vulgate transliterates the name as 'Man' (also in 16:33 and 16:35, echoing 'Manhu' in 16:15), rendered "Manna" / "manna" for clarity in English, and reads 'similae cum melle' ("fine flour with honey") where the Hebrew has "wafers with honey."
notes.16:34: The Vulgate distinctly reads 'in tabernaculo' ("in the tabernacle"), where the Hebrew reads "before the Testimony."
notes.17:7: Latin Tentatio ("Testing" or "Temptation") replaces the Hebrew dual place-name Massah and Meribah with a single translated name, absorbing the sense of Meribah into the explanatory phrase propter jurgium ("because of the dispute").
notes.17:12: Latin non lassarentur ("did not grow weary") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew states that the hands of Moses remained steady.
notes.17:15: Latin Dominus exaltatio mea ("The Lord Is My Exaltation") interprets the altar's name distinctively, where the Hebrew name means "the Lord is my banner."
notes.17:16: Latin manus solii Domini ("the hand of the throne of the Lord") renders a difficult Hebrew clause without a preposition before "throne," joining it with "the war of the Lord" as the subject of "will be against Amalek."
notes.18:1: Throughout chapter 18 the Vulgate consistently refers to Jethro as cognatus ("relative" or "kinsman") rather than socer ("father-in-law"), the term it used in Exodus 3:1 and 4:18 for the Hebrew choten.
notes.18:18: Latin Stulto labore consumeris ("You will be worn out with foolish labor") is a Vulgate-distinct reading reflecting a connection of the Hebrew verb navol ("wear out") with a homonymous root meaning "foolish."
notes.18:21: The Vulgate renders Israel's decimal judicial ranks with Roman military titles: tribunos (commanders of a thousand), centuriones (commanders of a hundred), quinquagenarios (leaders of fifty), and decanos (leaders of ten).
notes.18:23: Latin implebis imperium Dei, et praecepta ejus poteris sustentare ("you will fulfill the command of God, and you will be able to uphold His precepts") diverges from the Hebrew, which reads "and God so commands you, then you will be able to endure."
notes.19:6: Latin regnum sacerdotale ("a priestly kingdom") translates the Hebrew "kingdom of priests" with an adjective modifying "kingdom."
notes.19:18: Latin eratque omnis mons terribilis ("and the entire mountain was terrifying") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text states that the whole mountain trembled violently.
notes.19:19: Latin et Deus respondebat ei ("and God answered him") omits the Hebrew phrase "in thunder" (or "with a voice"), while expanding the trumpet description with et prolixius tendebatur ("and was drawn out longer").
notes.20:1: The Vulgate reads Dominus ("the Lord") rather than Hebrew Elohim ("God") and omits Hebrew "saying"; similarly, v. 19 reads "the Lord" for Hebrew "God."
notes.20:5: The Vulgate renders Hebrew El qanna ("a jealous God") as fortis, zelotes ("mighty, jealous"), translating El according to its sense of "mighty."
notes.20:13: Native Vulgate Exodus 20:13-15 order the prohibitions as killing (20:13), adultery (20:14), and theft (20:15); Saints.Bible parallel display maps to 20:15, 20:13, 20:14 respectively.
notes.20:18: Literally "saw the voices and the torches" (videbat voces et lampades), preserving the Vulgate's vivid portrayal of thunder as voices and lightning as fiery torches.
notes.20:25: Latin cultrum literally means "knife," rendering Hebrew cherev ("sword/knife"), here referring to an iron stone-cutting blade or tool.
notes.21:3: The Vulgate reads "with whatever clothing" (cum quali veste, and "with his clothing" in v. 4), whereas the Hebrew text reads "by himself" (literally "with his body/back").
notes.21:6: Latin diis literally means "to the gods," rendering plural Hebrew ha'elohim, which ancient interpreters often understood as "God" or as "the judges" acting in God's name.
notes.21:7: The Vulgate specifies "female slaves" (ancillae), whereas the Hebrew text reads "male slaves." In v. 10, the Vulgate likewise reads "marriage" (nuptias) and "price of chastity" (pretium pudicitiae) where the Hebrew lists sustenance and conjugal rights.
notes.21:16: Native Vulgate Exodus 21:16-17 place kidnapping in 21:16 and cursing parents in 21:17 (reverse of Saints.Bible Septuagint-aligned order 21:17 and 21:16). The Vulgate also reads "convicted of the offense" (convictus noxae) where the Hebrew reads "found in his possession."
notes.21:17: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate places cursing parents in v. 16 and kidnapping in v. 17, reversing the Hebrew Masoretic Text order. In v. 17, the Vulgate also reads "convicted of the offense" (convictus noxae) where the Hebrew reads "found in his possession."
notes.21:22: The Vulgate explicitly reads "suffers a miscarriage, yet she herself lives" (and "if her death follows" in v. 23), whereas the Hebrew reads "her children come out, yet there is no harm."
notes.22:1: Native Vulgate Exodus 22:1 maps to Saints.Bible 21:37, and native 22:2-31 map to Saints.Bible 22:1-30.
notes.22:3: The Vulgate explicitly states 'he has committed homicide, and he himself shall die' (homicidium perpetravit, et ipse morietur), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text states more briefly that there is bloodguilt for him before continuing with the thief's restitution.
notes.22:8: The Latin literally reads 'before the gods' (ad deos, echoed in 22:8 with plural 'if they pass judgment' and in 22:27 'revile the gods'), rendering Hebrew elohim in the plural; traditional Latin exegesis understood this to refer to judges acting under divine authority.
notes.22:18: The Vulgate uses the masculine plural 'sorcerers' (maleficos, practitioners of harmful magic), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses the feminine singular ('a sorceress').
notes.22:29: The Vulgate reads 'your tithes and your firstfruits' (decimas tuas et primitias tuas), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the fullness of the harvest and the outflow of the presses.
notes.22:31: The Vulgate reads meat 'tasted beforehand by wild animals' (a bestiis fuerit praegustata), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of flesh torn by beasts in the field.
notes.23:7: The Vulgate reads 'for I abhor the wicked' (quia aversor impium), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'for I will not acquit the wicked.'
notes.23:15: The Latin 'month of new crops' (mensis novorum) translates Hebrew chodesh ha-aviv ('month of Abib'), referring to the spring month of fresh ears of grain.
notes.23:25: The Vulgate uses first-person verbs ('so that I may bless... and remove', ut benedicam... et auferam), matching the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text shifts to the third person ('and he will bless') before returning to the first person.
notes.23:27: The Vulgate reads 'I will kill' (occidam), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'I will throw into confusion.'
notes.23:31: The Latin 'sea of the Philistines' (mare Palaestinorum) designates the Mediterranean Sea. In the final clause, the Vulgate reads in the first person ('and I will drive them out', et ejiciam eos), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads in the second person ('and you shall drive them out').
notes.24:11: Vulgate "qui procul recesserant" ("who had withdrawn to a distance") reflects Jerome's rendering of Hebrew "atsilei" (usually "nobles") from a root meaning "to set apart" or "withdraw."
notes.24:16: In the Vulgate, "gloria Domini" ("the glory of the Lord") is the subject of the participle "tegens" ("covering it with the cloud"), whereas the Hebrew makes the cloud the subject; "caliginis" ("thick darkness") and "nebulae" ("mist," v. 18) vary the repeated Hebrew word for "cloud."
notes.24:17: Latin "ignis ardens" literally means "burning fire," whereas the Hebrew reads "consuming/devouring fire."
notes.25:5: Vulgate "pelles janthinas" ("violet skins," following the Septuagint) differs from the uncertain Hebrew term "tachash" (variously "fine leather" or "porpoise skins"); "ligna setim" is Jerome's transliteration of Hebrew "shittim," meaning acacia wood.
notes.25:7: Latin "rationale" (lit., "rational" or "oracle-piece," translating Septuagint "logeion") denotes the high priest's breastpiece.
notes.25:18: Here and in v. 20 the Vulgate uses "oraculum" ("oracle") alongside "propitiatorium" ("mercy seat," vv. 17, 20, 22), whereas the Hebrew uses a single term ("kapporet") throughout.
notes.25:22: Vulgate "Inde praecipiam" ("From there I will give commands") differs from the Hebrew reading "there I will meet with you."
notes.25:29: Vulgate "thuribula" ("censers") is a distinctive Latin rendering for one of the golden table vessels.
notes.25:33: Latin "in nucis modum" and "instar nucis" ("in the shape/likeness of a nut") and "lilia" ("lilies," also vv. 31, 34) are Vulgate renderings where the Hebrew specifies almond-shaped cups and blossoms.
notes.26:1: The Vulgate renders the scarlet dye literally as 'twice-dyed scarlet' (cocco bis tincto) and describes the curtain design as 'variegated with embroidered work' (variatas opere plumario), without mentioning cherubim here or in 26:31 as the Hebrew and Septuagint do.
notes.26:14: Latin de janthinis pellibus ('of violet-colored skins') follows the Septuagint rendering of the obscure Hebrew term tahash, whose meaning is uncertain.
notes.26:15: Latin de lignis setim retains the transliterated Hebrew name shittim for the desert acacia tree, translated here and throughout as 'acacia wood'.
notes.26:28: The Vulgate uses the plural relative pronoun qui ('which'), referring to the bars generally passing through the middle of the boards, whereas the Hebrew specifies the single middle bar.
notes.26:32: Latin capita ('capitals' or 'heads') describes the tops of the pillars (as also in 26:37 and 27:10, 11, 17), where the Hebrew refers to 'hooks'.
notes.27:3: The Vulgate lists four altar utensils—pots, tongs (forcipes), forks, and receptacles for fire—whereas the Hebrew lists five, including shovels in place of tongs as well as basins.
notes.27:5: Latin quos ('these', masculine plural) refers grammatically to the bronze rings of 27:4 rather than the grating itself, and arulam (literally 'little altar' or 'hearth') corresponds to the Hebrew 'ledge'.
notes.27:10: Latin capita cum cælaturis suis ('capitals with their engravings', repeated in 27:11) corresponds to 'hooks and bands' in the Hebrew; likewise 27:17 describes the pillars as 'clad with silver plates' (vestitæ ... argenteis laminis).
notes.27:21: Latin in tabernaculo testimonii ('in the tabernacle of the testimony') follows the Septuagint reading rather than the Hebrew 'tent of meeting', and 'set it in place' (collocabunt) omits the Hebrew phrase 'from evening'.
notes.28:4: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew breastpiece as rationale (literally "rationale" or "piece of reason," echoing the Septuagint logeion) and the ephod descriptively as superhumerale ("shoulder vestment"). The Clementine Vulgate also reads the singular verb faciet ("he will make") here before shifting to plural Facient ("They will make") in the next sentence.
notes.28:13: Here and in 28:14 and 28:25, the Vulgate reads uncinos ("hooks"), whereas the Hebrew text describes gold filigree settings.
notes.28:30: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew Urim and Thummim interpretatively as Doctrinam et Veritatem ("Doctrine and Truth"), following the Septuagint's delosis kai aletheia.
notes.28:32: The Vulgate compares the woven neck-border to what is customarily made "at the outermost parts of garments" (in extremis vestium partibus), where the Hebrew text compares it to the opening of a coat of mail.
notes.28:43: The Vulgate reads tabernaculum testimonii ("tabernacle of the testimony"), following the Septuagint skene tou martyriou rather than the Hebrew "tent of meeting."
notes.29:5: Vulgate superhumerali ("shoulder vestment") and rationali ("breastpiece," literally "oracle-piece" reflecting Greek logeion) render the Hebrew ephod and breastpiece, and quod constringes balteo ("which you will fasten tightly with a sash") binds the breastpiece with a sash rather than girding Aaron with the woven band of the ephod as in the Hebrew.
notes.29:22: Vulgate armumque dextrum literally specifies the "right shoulder" (and similarly armum in 29:27), whereas the Hebrew text refers to the right thigh.
notes.29:33: Vulgate ut sit placabile sacrificium ("so that it may be an appeasing sacrifice") expresses the priests' meal as a purpose clause, whereas the Hebrew refers back to the consecrated food with which atonement was made.
notes.29:41: Vulgate et juxta ea quæ diximus ("and according to the things that We have spoken") uses a divine first-person plural to summarize the accompanying offerings, where the Hebrew explicitly mentions the drink offering.
notes.29:43: Vulgate reads præcipiam ("I will command") where the Hebrew has "I will meet," and explicitly specifies altare ("the altar") as what will be sanctified in God's glory.
notes.30:3: The Vulgate reads "its grate" (craticulam ejus), whereas the Hebrew text reads "its top" (or "roof").
notes.30:6: The Clementine Vulgate prints arcum (normally "arch" or "bow"), a known printing variant for arcam ("ark," as in 30:26 and 31:7), translated here as "ark" according to the intended sense.
notes.30:13: The Vulgate uses Roman and Greek reckoning terms: "passes by to be named" (transit ad nomen, a roll-call idiom), "measure of the temple" (mensuram templi, where the Hebrew has "shekel of the sanctuary"), and "obols" (obolos, for Hebrew gerahs).
notes.30:28: The Vulgate reads "and all the furnishings that pertain to their service" (et universam supellectilem quae ad cultum eorum pertinet) rather than naming the basin and its base here as in the Hebrew text.
notes.30:35: The Vulgate reads "carefully mixed" (mistum diligenter), whereas the Hebrew text reads "salted" (or "seasoned with salt").
notes.31:5: The Vulgate summarizes the stone- and wood-working crafts as "marble, and gems, and a variety of woods" (marmore, et gemmis, et diversitate lignorum), whereas the Hebrew specifies cutting stones for setting and carving wood.
notes.31:8: The Clementine Vulgate prints the genitive altaris ("of the altar"), a textual variant attracted to thymiamatis for the accusative altare ("the altar"), rendered here as the direct object "the altar of incense."
notes.31:14: The Vulgate reads "My Sabbath" (sabbatum meum) rather than "the Sabbath," and uses active morietur ("shall surely die," and "shall die" in 31:15) rather than the passive "shall be put to death" of the Hebrew.
notes.31:17: The Vulgate ends with "He ceased from work" (ab opere cessavit), omitting the additional Hebrew clause "and was refreshed."
notes.32:4: The Vulgate reads "by the work of casting" (opere fusorio), referring to metal casting, whereas the Hebrew reads "with an engraving tool."
notes.32:8: The Vulgate reads "the way that you showed them" (quam ostendisti eis), referring to Moses, whereas the Hebrew reads "the way that I commanded them."
notes.32:25: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "let loose" (or "out of control") as "stripped naked" (nudatus) and "had despoiled" (spoliaverat), and reads "on account of the disgrace of filth" (propter ignominiam sordis) where the Hebrew speaks of a derision among their enemies.
notes.32:28: The Vulgate reads "about twenty-three thousand men" (viginti tria millia), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Septuagint read "about three thousand men."
notes.33:5: The Vulgate expresses the threat as a direct future ("once I will go up in your midst and blot you out"), whereas the Hebrew is usually understood conditionally ("if for a single moment I should go up in your midst, I would consume you").
notes.33:7: The Vulgate calls the tent "the Tabernacle of the Covenant" (Tabernaculum foederis, rather than "tent of meeting") and reads "who had any question" (aliquam quaestionem) where the Hebrew reads "who sought the Lord."
notes.33:13: The Vulgate reads "show me Your face" (ostende mihi faciem tuam), linking directly to the Lord's replies in 33:14 and 33:20, whereas the Hebrew reads "make known to me Your ways."
notes.33:16: The Vulgate reads "so that we may be glorified by all the peoples" (ut glorificemur ab omnibus populis; aligning with the Septuagint, and also construable as "above all the peoples"), whereas the Hebrew reads "that we may be distinguished from all the peoples."
notes.33:22: The Vulgate specifies "My right hand" (dextera mea), whereas the Hebrew simply has "My palm" or "My hand."
notes.34:6: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, where the Lord proclaims His own name in the third person, the Vulgate renders this proclamation in the second person (v. 7: 'who keep... before You... who repay'), framing it as Moses' direct address to God ('Ruler, Lord God,' Latin Dominator Domine Deus) as the Lord passes before him.
notes.34:18: Instead of transliterating the Hebrew month name Abib, the Vulgate translates it descriptively first as 'the month of new crops' (mensis novorum) and then as 'the month of the spring season' (mense verni temporis).
notes.34:29: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew verb qaran ('shone, sent forth rays') as cornuta ('horned', from the related Hebrew root qeren, 'horn'), a reading repeated in vv. 30 and 35.
notes.34:35: Where the Hebrew text states that Moses replaced the veil until he went in to speak with the Lord, the Vulgate reads siquando loquebatur ad eos ('whenever he spoke to them').
notes.35:5: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for a sanctuary contribution (terumah) as primitias ('firstfruits'), here and in v. 21.
notes.35:7: The Vulgate renders the obscure Hebrew skin term tachash as janthinas ('violet-colored', also in v. 23).
notes.35:9: The Vulgate calls the high priest's ephod the superhumerale ('shoulder-vestment') and the breastpiece the rationale (literally 'piece of reason/judgment', calquing Greek logeion), here and in v. 27.
notes.35:35: The Vulgate specifies the artisans' crafts with the Latin triad abietarii, polymitarii, ac plumarii ('woodworker, tapestry-weaver, and embroiderer') and concludes with ac nova quæque reperiant ('and invent all kinds of new things').
notes.36:8: Native Vulgate Exodus 36:8-39:43 follow the Hebrew/Vulgate Tabernacle construction sequence (curtains, boards, ark, table, lampstand, altars, courtyard, priestly garments), differing from Saints.Bible Septuagint-aligned numbering in ch. 36-39. Stage 1 restored 37 native Vulgate verses previously dropped under the Greek-slotted anchor.
notes.36:19: Latin 'pellibus janthinis' ('violet-colored skins') renders Hebrew 'tachash' consistently with 25:5 and 35:7.
notes.36:35: Latin 'varium atque distinctum' (literally "variegated and distinct/adorned") describes the patterned weave of the veil without the reference to cherubim found in the Hebrew (Exod 36:35).
notes.37:1: Latin reads 'de lignis setim' (transliterating Hebrew 'shittim', acacia wood). In this chapter arrangement, the construction of the ark, table, and lampstand (placed in Exodus 37 in the Hebrew and standard Clementine Vulgate) appears in chapter 38.
notes.37:6: The Vulgate adds the explanatory gloss 'id est, oraculum' ('that is, the oracle'—the place of divine utterance) to 'propitiatorium' ('mercy seat'); this gloss has no counterpart in the Hebrew.
notes.37:19: The Vulgate describes the lampstand cups simply as shaped 'like a nut' ('in nucis modum' / 'instar nucis') and its ornaments as 'small spheres' ('sphaerulae') and 'lilies' ('lilia'), where the Hebrew specifies almond-shaped cups, calyxes/knobs, and blossoms.
notes.37:26: The Clementine Vulgate specifically reads "grate" (craticula) for the top surface of the incense altar.
notes.37:27: Latin coronam aureolam ("small gold crown") denotes the decorative gold molding around the upper edge of the altar.
notes.38:8: Latin 'quae excubabant' literally means 'who kept watch' (as on guard), a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew refers to women who assembled or served at the entrance.
notes.38:10: Both here and in v. 10, the Vulgate specifies "bronze pillars" ('columnae aeneae', where the Hebrew attributes bronze only to the bases), and renders the Hebrew hooks and bands as 'caelatura' ("engraved work" or "engravings," cf. vv. 10, 15, 17).
notes.38:17: The Vulgate states that the courtyard pillars themselves were covered with silver ('ipsas columnas atrii vestivit argento'), whereas the Hebrew refers to overlaying the tops of the pillars and making their bands of silver; similarly, v. 13 calls the courtyard entryway 'introitum tabernaculi' ("the entrance of the tabernacle").
notes.38:21: Latin 'instrumenta' ("furnishings") and 'in caeremoniis Levitarum' ("in the ceremonies of the Levites") represent what the Hebrew calls the records or inventory of the tabernacle for the service of the Levites (Exod 38:21).
notes.38:25: The Vulgate explicitly specifies 'armatorum' ('of armed men'), a clarifying detail not present in the Hebrew text.
notes.38:29: Following the Clementine Vulgate punctuation ('talenta septuaginta duo millia, et quadringenti supra sicli'), the Latin reads seventy-two thousand talents and four hundred shekels, whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint read seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels.
notes.39:1: This section follows the Septuagint-aligned verse ordering mapped to Vulgate text (corresponding to MT/standard Vulgate Exodus 39:1-31), moving directly from the offerings to the priestly garments. The Latin uses singular 'fecit' ("he made") through v. 17 before shifting to plural 'fecerunt' ("they made") in v. 22.
notes.39:2: Latin 'superhumerale' (literally "over-shoulder garment") renders the Hebrew 'ephod', and 'cocco bis tincto' ("twice-dyed scarlet," cf. v. 36) reflects an ancient reading of Hebrew 'shani' as "double."
notes.39:8: Latin 'rationale' (reflecting Greek 'logeion', "oracle-piece" or "piece of reason") denotes the high priest's breastpiece. In vv. 17-20, the Vulgate's names for the gems follow the Greek tradition rather than the Hebrew (for example, 'jaspis' in row two and 'beryllus' in row four, where the Hebrew has jasper last).
notes.39:24: The clause "with which the high priest walked adorned when he performed his ministry" ('quibus ornatus incedebat pontifex quando ministerio fungebatur') is a distinctive Vulgate expansion of the briefer Hebrew phrase ("for ministering").
notes.39:29: Latin 'laminam sacrae venerationis' ("the plate of sacred veneration") and the genitive inscription 'Sanctum Domini' ("Holiness of the Lord," matching Septuagint 'hagiasma Kyriou') differ slightly from the Hebrew ("plate of the holy diadem" inscribed "Holy to the Lord," cf. Vulgate Exod 28:36 'Sanctum Domino').
notes.39:33: Latin 'de janthinis pellibus' ('of violet-colored skins,' from Greek 'ianthinos') preserves a distinctive Vulgate and Septuagint color rendering of Hebrew 'tahash', a term of uncertain meaning.
notes.39:35: Latin 'propositionis panibus' literally means 'loaves of setting forth' or 'presentation' (following the Septuagint), corresponding to the 'bread of the Presence' in the Hebrew.
notes.40:11: Latin literally reads "Holy of holies" (Sancta sanctorum), expressing the superlative "most holy."
notes.40:13: The Vulgate condenses the Hebrew instructions for anointing Aaron and his sons (vv. 13-15) into the single clause 'et unctio eorum in sacerdotium sempiternum proficiat' ('and their anointing may serve for an everlasting priesthood').
notes.40:18: The Vulgate here calls the mercy seat simply 'oraculum' ('the oracle'), echoing its explanatory gloss in 38:5.
notes.40:30: Latin 'tectum foederis' ('tent of the covenant,' where 'tectum' literally means 'covering' or 'roof') is Jerome's distinctive rendering for what the Hebrew calls the 'tent of meeting.'
notes.40:33: The Vulgate distinctively renders the divine presence as 'majestate Domini coruscante' ('the majesty of the Lord flashing forth') and states twice that the cloud covered everything ('nube operiente omnia ... quia cuncta nubes operuerat').
notes.40:34: Latin 'per turmas suas' ('by their companies') is a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew reads 'throughout all their journeys'; similarly, 40:38 reads plural 'populis Israel' ('peoples of Israel') and 'mansiones' ('encampments') where the Hebrew reads 'house of Israel' and 'journeys.'
